title: 'The Relique': relics and the Reformation
short: Relics are a saint's bodily remains, venerated in Catholic devotion; Protestant England had destroyed most shrines under Henry VIII and Edward VI.
body: The poem imagines the lovers' bones dug up and venerated as relics in some future age of 'mis-devotion'. In Donne's England relic-cults had been suppressed and shrines destroyed since the 1530s, but Donne, raised a Catholic, knew the practices well. The poem plays with Catholic devotion while seeming to scorn it. First printed in 1633. Grierson thought it Platonic rather than Petrarchan in spirit and suggested it was addressed to Magdalen Herbert, mother of George Herbert and Lord Herbert of Cherbury, whom Donne knew well from about 1607.

sources.cite: H. J. C. Grierson, ed., The Poems of John Donne (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1912), vol. II, commentary on 'The Relique'

title: grave ... broke up againe
short: Graves were routinely reopened and the bones moved to charnel houses so the ground could be reused.
body: In crowded churchyards graves were reopened for new burials and old bones removed to the charnel house (compare the gravediggers in Hamlet V.i). Donne's sermons dwell often on the scattering and mingling of the dead in the earth. The opening is abrupt and macabre, and the poem moves from this grim future to the lovers' hoped-for meeting at the Resurrection. 'Ghest' (guest) treats the second corpse as a visitor to be 'entertained', preparing the joke of the next lines.

title: woman-head
short: Womanhood, womanly nature: graves have learned the female trick of being a bed to more than one.
body: 'Woman-head' is an old form of 'womanhood' (OED). The cynical parenthesis, typical of the Songs and Sonets, imputes promiscuity to women in general, even as the poem goes on to praise one woman's chaste love. The tension between misogynist wit and idealising devotion is characteristic of Donne and has been much discussed by feminist critics, among them Ilona Bell in her Cambridge Companion chapter, 'Gender matters: the women in Donne's poems'.

title: A bracelet of bright haire about the bone
short: A lock of the lady's hair worn around the speaker's wrist, a love token buried with him.
body: Gifts of hair were common love tokens. Grierson, discussing 'The Funerall', links this poem with that one, where 'That subtile wreath of haire, which crowns my arme' guards the speaker's body. In 'The Relique' the striking line juxtaposes the bright hair with the bare bone, the living token with mortality. The image also connects with the Magdalen, traditionally depicted with long hair.

title: the last busie day
short: Judgement Day, when all the dead rise and souls must find and reassemble their scattered bodies.
body: At the general resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:51-52; Revelation 20:12-13) souls were expected to rejoin their bodies; theologians debated how scattered particles would be gathered. The day is 'busie' because of all this collecting. The lovers' device is that the bracelet will make the lady's soul come to his grave in search of her hair, so that their souls 'meet' and 'make a little stay'. Donne treats the resurrection of the body at length in his sermons.

title: mis-devotion
short: Misguided worship, i.e. Catholic veneration of relics. The 1669 editor's 'Mass-devotion' is, Grierson says, merely a conjecture.
body: Grierson keeps 'mis-devotion', the reading of the earlier editions and the manuscripts, and rejects 1669's 'Mass-devotion' as an ingenious editorial guess; he shows Donne using 'mis-devotion' elsewhere. The word places the poem in a Protestant frame: only in a time or land of false devotion would bones be made relics. The speaker's tone is ambiguous, since he plainly relishes the prospect.

anchor: to the Bishop, and the King
title: the Bishop, and the King
short: Ecclesiastical and royal authority, who would examine and approve the relics, as in pre-Reformation and Catholic practice.
body: In a Catholic setting, the bishop would authenticate relics and the king might sponsor a shrine. The pairing glances at the union of church and state that controlled religion in Donne's own England, where the monarch was Supreme Governor of the Church and bishops enforced conformity. The ironic picture of solemn authorities venerating two lovers' bones is part of the poem's comedy.

anchor: Thou shalt be a Mary Magdalen
title: a Mary Magdalen
short: The penitent woman of the Gospels, traditionally (though not biblically) identified as a reformed prostitute, shown with long flowing hair.
body: Western tradition merged Mary Magdalene (Mark 16:9; John 20) with the sinful woman who wiped Christ's feet with her hair (Luke 7:37-38), hence her iconography of long hair, which the bracelet recalls. Grierson notes that some manuscripts read 'You shalbe', explains Donne's use of 'thou' as the pronoun of feeling and intimacy, and suggests the poem was addressed to Mrs Magdalen Herbert. The comparison is double-edged: a famous saint, but one with a sinful past.

title: A something else
short: The speaker leaves his own relic-identity teasingly unnamed: perhaps a lover of the Magdalen, perhaps, daringly, Christ.
body: If she is Mary Magdalen, the obvious partner is Christ, and many readers find the vagueness a deliberate evasion of blasphemy. Others note medieval legends that made the Magdalen the bride of St John, or simply hear a mock-modest shrug. The next line, 'All women shall adore us, and some men', adds a further joke: women would worship the Magdalen, but only 'some men' the speaker.

title: this paper
short: The poem itself, imagined as a document buried with the relics to explain the lovers' 'miracles'.
body: Since such an age will seek miracles to authenticate its saints, the speaker leaves 'this paper' to set the record straight, as relics were accompanied by written authentication. The 'miracles' of 'harmelesse lovers' (innocent, doing no harm) turn out to be the paradoxes of a chaste love, listed in stanza 3. 'Taught' carries a teasing note: the speaker means to correct the future Church's errors about his own sainthood. The paper is also the speaker's claim that poetry, not relics, preserves the lovers' story.

title: Difference of sex ... Guardian Angells
short: Like angels, who are sexless, the lovers paid no attention to sexual difference. 'New' here represents 'knew' (Grierson's reading).
body: Angels were held to be without sex (compare Matthew 22:30: in the resurrection they 'neither marry, nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God'). Each person was believed to have a guardian angel (Matthew 18:10). The lovers' love is thus angelic. Note that this archive prints 'wee new'; Grierson's text reads 'wee knew', and the sense requires 'knew'.

title: Comming and going ... kisse ... meales
short: They kissed only in greeting and farewell, as English custom allowed; Grierson cites Erasmus on this English habit.
body: Grierson explains the kisses as those of salutation and parting, quotes a Donne sermon on the kiss, and cites Erasmus's letter of 1499 describing the English custom of kissing on arrival and departure. 'Between those meales' treats kisses as nourishment: they took their kisses only at the proper 'mealtimes' of meeting and leaving. The kisses are thus within social propriety, a sign of the love's chastity.

anchor: Our hands ne'r toucht the seales
title: the seales
short: The 'seals' of love: the parts of the body, or sexual consummation, that seal a contract of love.
body: A seal confirms a legal document, and 'seals of love' was a common figure for kisses or for the sexual act that consummates a bond. The lovers never 'touched the seals', that is, never consummated their love. The image belongs with the legal language of 'late law' in the following line. Some editors take the seals more concretely as the private parts, which nature 'sets free'.

title: Which nature, injur'd by late law, sets free
greek: Latin (Ovid) 'quod natura remittit, / invida iura negant'
short: Nature permits sexual love freely; only later, man-made law restricts it. Compare Myrrha's complaint in Ovid's Metamorphoses 10.
body: The line appeals to a 'state of nature' before custom and positive law, when love was free. Editors compare Ovid, Metamorphoses 10.329-31, where Myrrha complains that what nature allows, envious laws forbid; the idea also appears in Tasso's Aminta and in Donne's own 'Elegy: Variety'. The lovers did not take the liberty nature grants, which is their 'miracle'. The line's sympathy with nature against law sits uneasily with the poem's celebration of chastity, an irony critics have noted.

sources.cite: Ovid, Metamorphoses 10.329-31

title: what a miracle shee was
short: The lovers' 'miracles' are listed, but the greatest is the woman herself, beyond all measure and language.
body: The final lines move from 'wee' to 'shee': the real miracle is the beloved, whom no measure (metre, and moderation) or language could describe. The modesty topos (inexpressibility) closes a poem that has mocked relic-worship by itself canonising her. The ending contrasts with the cynical 'woman-head' of l. 3. Each stanza has eleven lines of varied length, rhyming aabbcddceee, and ends on a triplet, here 'alas / passe / was'.
